tagline: Switchbacks descend from sage country to carved rock and sandstone towers.
intro: The Indian Creek Corridor Scenic Byway leaves US 191 north of Monticello, crosses a high sage plain and drops through tight turns into Indian Creek Canyon. Utah’s Canyon Country promotes the drive for Newspaper Rock’s petroglyphs and the canyon journey toward the Needles District of Canyonlands National Park. The whole of SR 211 carries the scenic-byway designation. Much of the open land beside the route belongs to The Nature Conservancy’s Dugout Ranch, whose private acreage is associated with extensive public grazing allotments.

In 1968, Utah’s State Road Commission, the National Park Service and San Juan County agreed to improve the unpaved Needles access road. The SR 211 designation was deleted in 1969 and restored in 1971. After construction, the state highway reached Dugout Ranch; the remaining stretch to the park boundary stayed a county road. A later interruption came when heavy rain destroyed much of the road in August 2022; it reopened that September.

Travel west past Home of Truth and through Photograph Gap before descending to Newspaper Rock, directly beside the highway. Beyond the panel, Bridger Jack Butte is visible from the road toward the Needles. The canyon opens into a broad valley, and the byway continues to the park district.

moments.title: Home of Truth
moments.text: Empty buildings behind fences beside SR 211 mark Home of Truth, the religious community Marie Ogden started in 1933. Residents surrendered their possessions to the group and built their own houses and furniture. Ogden bought the San Juan Record in 1934 and used it to promote her beliefs. Her claims that a deceased member could return to life brought investigations and press attention; most members left by the end of 1937. A few residents remained until 1977. The settlement had three sections spread from east to west, with at least 23 buildings constructed across the site.

moments.title: Newspaper Rock
moments.text: More than 650 designs cover Newspaper Rock, including human figures, animals and abstract forms. The artists chipped through dark desert varnish to expose the lighter sandstone beneath. Older figures are darkening again as new varnish develops. Deer, buffalo and pronghorn appear among the carvings, along with riders on horses. The panel belongs to the Wingate sandstone cliffs enclosing the upper end of Indian Creek Canyon. The reason so many carvings accumulated here remains unclear, and their precise dates are difficult to establish. The carved surface occupies 200 square feet of a vertical rock face, bringing many different figures together within one panel.
moments.notice: The carved figures expose lighter rock beneath dark desert varnish; older figures have begun to darken again.

moments.title: Bridger Jack Butte
moments.text: Bridger Jack Butte rises more than 700 feet above the surrounding terrain and Lavender Canyon, above the meeting of Indian and Lavender creeks. Its hard Wingate Sandstone formed from windblown dunes deposited approximately 200 million years ago. That resistant rock makes steep cliffs above softer layers of the Chinle Formation. Below the Chinle lies the Moenkopi Formation, adding another named layer to the butte’s geological foundation. The butte stands at the northern tip of Bridger Jack Mesa; towers called the Bridger Jacks occupy the connecting ridge. It is visible from SR 211 between Newspaper Rock and the Needles District.

practical: Newspaper Rock: On SR 211, the Utah Department of Transportation requires a pilot car escort for vehicles wider than 10 feet or longer than 80 feet. (checked 2026-10-11)
